sections.title: Phonological Similarity Effect
original: The phonological similarity effect: lists of similar-sounding items are recalled worse than lists of different-sounding items, even when the items are only read silently. Acoustic similarity effect is arguably the better name.

So people recode what they see into a speech-based form. A purely visual code would cause mix-ups between look-alikes such as E and F instead. This is the basis of the phonological loop in working memory.

The loop has a phonological store and an articulatory control process that converts visual input to speech and refreshes traces. Articulatory suppression occupies that process, and with visually presented lists the similarity cost disappears.

v20.text: The **phonological similarity effect** is the finding that people recall a list **worse when its items sound alike** than when they sound different. What matters is how the items sound to each other, which is why **acoustic similarity effect** is arguably the better name.
children: The surprising part is that it still happens when you **read the items silently**, with no sound at all.
Conrad (1964) reported the effect.

v20.text: Because silent reading still produces it, we must be **recoding visual information into a speech-based form**. If memory used only a visual code, we would confuse items that **look** alike, such as E and F, rather than items that **sound** alike.
children: This recoding idea is central to Baddeley's (1986) **phonological loop**, a component of **working memory**.

v20.text: The loop has two parts: a **phonological store** that briefly holds speech-based traces, and an **articulatory control process** that turns visual input into a speech code and refreshes the traces.
children: Murray (1968) used **articulatory suppression**, in which the control process is kept busy, so visual items cannot be recoded.
With recoding blocked, the loop predicts that similar-sounding and different-sounding visually presented lists are **recalled equally well**.

v21.text: Items that **sound alike** are harder to recall in a list than items that sound different. This is the **phonological similarity effect**, which could just as well be called the **acoustic** similarity effect.
children: It holds even for **silent reading**, so no sound has to be presented.

v21.text: The best reading is that we **convert what we see into a speech code**. With a purely visual code the mix-ups would be between look-alikes such as E and F.
children: That logic is the foundation of the **phonological loop** in working memory.

v21.text: The loop pairs a **phonological store** for short-lived speech traces with an **articulatory control process** that recodes visual input and refreshes traces.
children: Keeping that process busy (**articulatory suppression**) blocks recoding, and for visually presented lists the sound-alike cost goes away.

v22.text: Conrad (1964) found that items that **sound alike** are harder to recall as a list than items that sound different, the **phonological similarity effect**; sound is what matters, so **acoustic similarity effect** is arguably the better name.
children: It holds even for **silent reading**, so no sound has to be presented.

v22.text: The best reading is that we **convert what we see into a speech code**. With a purely visual code the mix-ups would be between look-alikes such as E and F.
children: Baddeley (1986) built the **phonological loop** of working memory on this logic.

v22.text: The loop pairs a **phonological store** for short-lived speech traces with an **articulatory control process** that recodes visual input and refreshes traces.
children: Murray (1968) kept that process busy with **articulatory suppression** to block recoding; with visually presented lists the sound-alike cost goes away.

sections.title: Neighborhood Size Effect
original: A word's neighborhood is the set of words that differ from it by one letter (orthographic) or one sound (phonological): cat is a large neighborhood word, hippopotamus a small neighborhood word.
Roodenrys et al. (2002) found that large neighborhood words are recalled better in short-term memory tasks, so long-term memory knowledge of words helps short-term recall.
As a result, memory span is not a pure measure of short-term capacity.

v20.text: The **neighborhood size effect** is a case where **long-term memory factors change short-term memory**. A word's neighborhood is every word you get by changing one letter (**orthographic**) or one sound (**phonological**).
children: Cat has lots of neighbors, such as bat, cot and can, so it is a **large neighborhood word**; hippopotamus has none, so it is a **small neighborhood word**.

v20.text: Roodenrys et al. (2002) found that in a standard short-term memory task people **recall more large neighborhood words than small neighborhood words**.
children: So what you know about the language, stored in long-term memory, changes performance on a short-term task.

v20.text: That causes trouble for **memory span**. If span is affected by long-term memory, it **cannot be a pure measure of short-term memory capacity**.

v21.text: How well a word is held in **short-term memory** depends on how many similar words it has, which is a **long-term memory** influence: the **neighborhood size effect**.
children: Neighbors are words one letter (orthographic) or one sound (phonological) away; cat has many (**large neighborhood**), hippopotamus has none (**small neighborhood**).

v21.text: Words from **large neighborhoods are recalled better** than words from small neighborhoods.
children: Language knowledge is shaping short-term performance.

v21.text: So **memory span** cannot be a clean measure of short-term capacity, because long-term memory contributes to it.

v22.text: Roodenrys et al. (2002) showed that **long-term memory factors affect short-term memory**: a word's **neighborhood**, the words one letter (orthographic) or one sound (phonological) away, changes how well it is recalled.
children: Cat has many neighbors (**large neighborhood**); hippopotamus has none (**small neighborhood**).

v22.text: In their short-term memory task, **large neighborhood words were recalled better** than small neighborhood words.
children: Stored knowledge about words is boosting short-term performance.

v22.text: Therefore **memory span** cannot be a clean measure of short-term capacity, because long-term memory contributes to it.

sections.title: Brown-Peterson Task
original: In the Brown-Peterson task people study consonants and then do a distractor task, counting backwards, that blocks rehearsal. The longer the distraction, the worse the recall.

Because counting is so unlike remembering letters, Peterson and Peterson (1959) judged interference an unlikely cause and concluded that short-term memory (STM) loses information through decay unless it is rehearsed.

This challenged the view, following McGeoch's (1932) critique, that forgetting is due to interference; decay is the researchers' conclusion, and Keppel and Underwood (1962) are cited for an alternative.

v20.text: The **Brown-Peterson task** was used to show that **information in short-term memory is forgotten quickly when rehearsal is prevented**. After McGeoch's (1932) influential critique, forgetting had been put down to **interference** and not decay.
children: Peterson and Peterson (1959) had people see a few consonants and then do a hard **distractor task**, counting backwards, so they could not rehearse the letters.

v20.text: The longer the distractor lasted, the **less likely people were to recall the letters**.
children: Counting backwards is very different from remembering letters, so Peterson and Peterson judged interference an unlikely explanation.

v20.text: Their conclusion was that there is a **short-term memory (STM) system** that holds information only briefly, and that without rehearsal the information **fades away (decay)**.
children: That is their claim; Keppel and Underwood (1962) are cited as offering an alternative explanation of the results.

v21.text: The **Brown-Peterson task** pairs studying a few letters with a **distractor task**, such as counting backwards, that stops rehearsal.
children: The longer the distraction, the **worse the recall**.

v21.text: Counting is so unlike remembering letters that the researchers judged **interference** an unlikely cause of the forgetting.
They concluded that **short-term memory (STM)** holds information only briefly and loses it through **decay** unless it is rehearsed.
children: This ran against the earlier view that forgetting is due to **interference**, not decay.

v22.text: In the **Brown-Peterson task** people studied a few letters and then did a **distractor task**, counting backwards, that stopped rehearsal; Peterson and Peterson (1959) found that the longer the distraction, the **worse the recall**.
children: Counting is so unlike remembering letters that they judged **interference** an unlikely cause.

v22.text: Their conclusion was that **short-term memory (STM)** holds information only briefly and loses it through **decay** unless it is rehearsed.
children: This went against the view that followed McGeoch's (1932) critique, that forgetting is due to **interference**.

v22.text: Decay is the original researchers' conclusion, not the only reading: Keppel and Underwood (1962) are cited as offering an alternative explanation.

sections.title: Modality Effect
original: The modality effect: better memory for the last one or two items of a list when it is heard than when it is read silently. Lip-read or silently mouthed lists show it too.
It strongly influenced ideas about sensory memory, a back-up store of raw, unanalyzed sensory input.
The favored explanation (Neath and Surprenant, 2003) is that hearing adds extra information about how the list sounds, which helps the final items.

v20.text: The **modality effect** is an advantage for the **last one or two items** of a list when the list is **heard** rather than read silently.
children: It also appears for lists that are **lip-read or silently mouthed**, so it is not only about hearing.

v20.text: These findings had a big influence on the idea of **sensory memory**, a system supposed to hold **raw, unanalyzed sensory input** as a back-up that can improve recall when its information is useful.
The favored explanation, from Neath and Surprenant (2003), is that **auditory presentation provides an additional type of information** compared with visual presentation.
children: When recalling the last items, you do better if you also have information about **how the list sounded**.

v21.text: Hearing a list gives better memory for its **final one or two items** than reading it silently. That is the **modality effect**.
children: Lists that are lip-read or mouthed give the same benefit.

v21.text: The effect pushed theorists toward **sensory memory**: a back-up store of **raw, unanalyzed input** that helps when that information is useful.
The favored account is that hearing supplies **extra information about how the items sound**, and that extra information supports the end of the list.

v22.text: The **modality effect** is a memory advantage for the **last one or two items** of a **heard** list over a silently read one, and it also shows up with lip-read or mouthed lists.
It strongly shaped thinking about **sensory memory**, a back-up store holding **raw, unanalyzed sensory input** that can help recall.
Neath and Surprenant (2003) give the favored explanation: **hearing adds a further kind of information**, how the list sounds, and this helps the final items.

sections.title: Partial Report
original: Early work suggested people can report only a small part of a brief display. Sperling (1960) argued that this limit comes from recall, not perception.
With partial report, a cue right after the display lets observers report the cued part almost perfectly, so a sensory (iconic) store briefly held nearly all of it.
The real limit is the time needed to report: delay the cue and performance falls toward the usual limit, because the store is very short-lived.

v20.text: Early researchers studying the **perceptual span** found that people could report only a small part of a brief glance, and this limit was built into many theories. Sperling (1960) suggested it came from **observers' ability to recall** what they had seen, not from perception.
children: He used the **partial-report** method, where a cue after the display tells observers which part to report.

v20.text: When the cue came **right after the display disappeared**, observers reported the cued part almost perfectly, whichever part it was.
children: So a **sensory (iconic) store** briefly held nearly a complete copy of the display.

v20.text: The real limit is the **time needed to report**, because the store fades while observers are reporting.
children: When the cue was **delayed**, performance fell back toward the usual limit, which shows how **briefly** the store lasts.

v21.text: What limits report from a brief glance is **recall**, not perception: observers see far more than they can report.
The evidence is **partial report**. A cue pointing to one part of the display just after it vanishes lets that part be reported almost perfectly, whichever part it is.
children: So a **sensory (iconic) store** briefly holds almost everything that was seen.

v21.text: Delay the cue and the advantage fades, so the store is **very short-lived**. The bottleneck is the **time it takes to report**, during which items fade.

v22.text: Sperling (1960) challenged the idea that perception caps how much we take in from a brief glance. The cap, he argued, is on **recall**.
His **partial-report** method cued observers toward one part of the display as it vanished, and whichever part was cued came out nearly intact.
children: That implies a **sensory (iconic) store** briefly held almost the whole display.

v22.text: A delayed cue lost the advantage, so the store **fades quickly**, and full report is limited because items disappear **while being reported**.

sections.title: Position Error Effect
original: The position error effect: items are usually recalled in the correct position, and when they are not, the errors are systematic, with the item landing in an adjacent position.
So order errors are not random, and scoring only percent correct hides that people keep approximate position information.

v20.text: The **position error effect** is about remembering **order** as well as items, such as the digits of a phone number. Most of the time an item is **recalled in its correct position**.
children: When a mistake is made, it is **systematic and predictable**, not random.

v20.text: A misplaced item most likely comes out in an **adjacent position**. An item that is not recalled third is probably recalled second or fourth, and rarely far from where it belongs.
This matters because **percent correct alone makes forgetting look like lost information**. In fact people still remember **roughly where the item belonged**.

v21.text: Memory for **order** is mostly right, and the mistakes follow a **pattern**: a misplaced item tends to end up **next to its true slot** and seldom far away.
Because the errors are not random, people clearly keep **approximate position information**. Counting only **percent correct** treats a near miss as complete forgetting and hides this.

v22.text: Order memory shows a clear pattern: each item most often comes back in its own slot.
When it does not, the item usually lands one place away, so the third item of a list is more likely to appear second or fourth than first or last. The errors are **systematic**, not random.
That means forgetting a position is **not the same as losing the item**. Percent correct alone makes it look like **lost information**, but people retain **approximate position information**.

sections.title: Mental Rotation
original: People seem to use mental images, but self-reports of imagery are unreliable: it is impossible to tell whether the images differ or only the descriptions. So researchers use tasks that require imagery and vary a critical part of the task.

Shepard and Metzler (1971) had people judge whether two block shapes were the same or mirror images, with one turned. People mentally rotated one shape, and the larger the turn, the longer the response, at a constant rate.
This suggests mental images are much like real images, and it influenced theories of mental representation.

v20.text: The main theme is that **mental images behave like real images**. When we count the windows in our home, we seem to move through a **mental image**, but asking people to describe their images does not tell us much, since we cannot tell whether the images differ or only the descriptions do.
children: So researchers use **tasks that require imagery** and change one critical part of the task, which lets them work out objectively what images are like.

v20.text: **Shepard and Metzler (1971)** showed people two unfamiliar block shapes and asked whether they were the **same shape or mirror images**, with one shape turned relative to the other. People said they **mentally rotated** one shape until it lined up with the other.
children: The **more one shape was turned away from the other, the longer people took** to respond.
That extra time grew at a steady, **constant rate**, as if the image turned at a fixed speed.

v20.text: So **rotating a mental image takes time**, just as turning a real object does, which suggests **mental images are much like real images**.
children: These findings had a large influence on **theories of mental representation**.

v21.text: Descriptions of our own mental images are a poor guide, because there is no way to tell whether the **images** differ or only the **descriptions** do. So we need a task that forces people to use imagery and shows it in their behavior.
children: Counting the windows in your home is the kind of everyday task where we seem to inspect a **mental image**.

v21.text: In the classic rotation task people judged whether two block shapes were the **same or mirror images** when one was turned. They said they **mentally rotated** one shape to match the other.
children: The **bigger the turn, the longer the judgment**, and the extra time rose at a **constant rate**.

v21.text: Rotating an image takes time, as with a real object, which suggests **mental images are much like real images**, an idea that shaped **theories of mental representation**.

v22.text: Self-descriptions of mental images are unreliable, so imagery is studied with tasks that force it, as in Shepard and Metzler (1971). People judged whether two block shapes were the **same or mirror images** when one was turned, and said they **mentally rotated** one shape to match the other.
children: The **bigger the turn, the longer the judgment**, and the extra time rose at a **constant rate**.

v22.text: Everyday tasks such as counting the windows in your home seem to rely on a **mental image**, and these results suggest such images are treated **much like real images**.
children: Rotating an image takes time, as with a real object.

v22.text: Shepard and Metzler's (1971) findings shaped **theories of mental representation**.

sections.title: Typical Reasoning
original: People judge probability with heuristics that trade accuracy for speed: usually good enough, but sometimes wrong. Tversky and Kahneman (1983) showed estimates often differ greatly from objective probability.
The conjunction fallacy is judging that A and B together are more likely than A alone or B alone, although a combination is never more likely than either part alone.
Shafir, Smith, and Osherson (1990) found that people sometimes rated a combination of professions or activities as more likely than one part, which points to heuristics rather than probability rules.

v20.text: The main theme is that people judge probability with **heuristics**, which **trade some accuracy for speed**. Heuristics are usually good enough for day-to-day purposes, but they can lead to **incorrect judgments**.
children: **Tversky and Kahneman (1983)** showed that people's estimates of probability often differ greatly from objective probabilities.

v20.text: A striking example is the **conjunction fallacy**, thinking that **both A and B together are more likely than A alone or B alone**.
children: By objective probability, two events together can **never be more likely than** either one on its own, yet people sometimes judge otherwise.

v20.text: **Shafir, Smith, and Osherson (1990)** gave people short descriptions of a person and asked how likely it was that the person had certain professions or took part in certain activities. People sometimes rated the **combination as more likely than one part of it**.
children: This supports the idea that people rely on **heuristics** rather than the rules of probability.

v21.text: Probability judgments run on **heuristics**: fast shortcuts that give up some accuracy. They work day to day but can produce **wrong judgments**, and people's estimates often stray far from the true odds.
The **conjunction fallacy** shows it. People say that **A and B together** is more likely than A alone or B alone, even though a combination is **never more likely than** either part.

In studies where people read a short description of a person and rated how likely certain professions or activities were, they sometimes rated the **combination above a single part**, which shows reliance on **heuristics**, not probability rules.

v22.text: Tversky and Kahneman (1983) showed that probability judgments run on **heuristics**: fast shortcuts that give up some accuracy. They work day to day but can produce **wrong judgments**.
The **conjunction fallacy** shows it. People say that **A and B together** is more likely than A alone or B alone, even though a combination is **never more likely than** either part.

Shafir, Smith, and Osherson (1990) had people read a short description of a person and rate how likely certain professions or activities were. They sometimes rated the **combination above a single part**, which shows reliance on **heuristics**, not probability rules.

sections.title: Wason Selection
original: In the Wason Selection Task, the rule "If a card has a D on one side, it has a 3 on the other" is best tested with D and 7, since the 7 could falsify it. Most people choose D and 3, and the 3 can only confirm the rule.
The same logic in a familiar thematic rule ("If you borrow my car, you must fill up the gas tank") is much easier: choose "borrowed car" and "empty gas tank."
Wason and Shapiro (1971) compared abstract and thematic rules: people test a rule well with relevant experience, and abstract rules force them to use logic alone.

v20.text: People find it hard to test an **abstract rule**. In the **Wason Selection Task**, the rule is "If a card has a D on one side, it has a 3 on the other side," and the job is to choose the cards that could show the rule is broken.
children: The correct cards are **D and 7**, because a D without a 3, or a 7 with a D behind it, would **falsify** the rule.
Most people pick D and 3, but the 3 card can only **confirm** the rule, since the rule says nothing about what must be behind a 3.

v20.text: A rule with the same logical form but familiar content, such as "If you borrow my car, you must fill up the gas tank," is **much easier**.
children: The right cards are **"borrowed car" and "empty gas tank,"** because those could reveal someone who borrowed the car and did not fill it.

v20.text: **Wason and Shapiro (1971)** compared abstract and thematic rules. People can test a rule when they have **knowledge or experience** that fits it.
children: With thematic rules people use **experience, not logic per se**; with abstract rules they must rely **solely on logic**.

v21.text: The card rule "If D on one side, then 3 on the other" is tested by the cards that could **break** it: **D and 7**.
children: People tend to turn D and 3, but the 3 can only **confirm** the rule, and they miss the 7, which could **falsify** it.

v21.text: Put the same logic in a familiar rule such as "If you borrow my car, you must fill up the tank," and it becomes **easy**: check the borrowed car and the empty tank.
Abstract and thematic versions were compared. **Relevant experience** makes a rule testable; without it people must use **logic alone**.

v22.text: The **Wason Selection Task** asks which cards to turn over to check "If a card has a D on one side, it has a 3 on the other." Only **D and 7** could **falsify** it.
children: A common choice is D and 3, yet the 3 can only **confirm** the rule, while the 7 goes unchecked.

v22.text: A familiar rule with identical logic, "If you borrow my car, you must fill up the tank," is **far easier**, since the borrowed car and the empty tank are the obvious cards to check.
Wason and Shapiro (1971) compared abstract with thematic rules and concluded that **relevant experience** lets people test a rule, whereas abstract rules leave only **logic**.

sections.title: Decision Making
original: Decisions are influenced by many factors, and framing effects occur when the wording or context makes a big difference to a choice, even for otherwise equivalent situations. Kahneman and Tversky (1982) summarized many of them.
The same choice can be presented in two ways. In classic framing research (Tversky and Kahneman), gain wording typically leads to the sure option and loss wording to the gamble.
So choices can follow the framing and not the substance.

v20.text: The main theme is that **decisions are shaped by how a choice is framed**, not only by what the options are. People would like to weigh their options carefully, but many tendencies, called **framing effects**, push them in particular directions.
children: It is fairly easy to create a context in which people choose a particular option.

v20.text: In a **framing effect**, the **perceived context or wording of the choice** makes a big difference, even when the situations are **otherwise equivalent**.
children: **Kahneman and Tversky (1982)** summarized many framing effects.

v20.text: The same choice can be presented in **two different ways**, and people choose differently depending on the version.
children: In classic framing research (Tversky and Kahneman), **gain wording** typically pushes people toward the **sure option** and **loss wording** toward the **gamble**, so the choice follows the framing and not the substance.

v21.text: **How a choice is framed shapes the decision**, not just the options themselves, and many such tendencies are called **framing effects**. It is fairly easy to set up a context that steers people.
What defines a **framing effect** is that the **wording or context** changes the choice even though the situations are **otherwise equivalent**.

Show the same choice in **two different ways** and people choose differently. In the classic framing studies, **gain wording** typically leads to the **sure option** and **loss wording** to the **gamble**.

v22.text: **How a choice is framed shapes the decision**, not just the options themselves. Kahneman and Tversky (1982) summarized many of these **framing effects**.
What defines a **framing effect** is that the **wording or context** changes the choice even though the situations are **otherwise equivalent**.

Tversky and Kahneman's classic framing studies showed the same choice in **two different ways**, and **gain wording** typically led to the **sure option** while **loss wording** led to the **gamble**.

sections.title: Monty Hall
original: The Monty Hall 3 Door problem shows poor intuition about the probability of combinations of events. After you pick one of three doors, the host, who always plays fair this way, opens a no-prize door.
Many people think stay or switch makes no difference, which is incorrect: you should switch, which wins about two-thirds of the time.
Your first pick keeps its 1 in 3 chance, so the 2 in 3 held by the other two doors moves to the one remaining door.

v20.text: The main theme is that **intuition about probability is often wrong**, and the **Monty Hall 3 Door problem** is the classic example. A prize is behind one of three doors, you pick one, and Monty Hall, who is assumed to play fair and always do this, opens one of the other two doors to show **no prize**. Should you **stay or switch**?
children: Many people think it does not matter, which is **incorrect**.

v20.text: **The right choice is to switch.** Always switching wins about **two-thirds** of the time and always staying wins about **one-third**.
children: Most people miss this because they treat the two remaining doors as equally likely.

v20.text: Your first pick has a **1 in 3 chance** of being right, so there is a **2 in 3 chance** the prize is behind one of the other two doors.
children: When Monty Hall shows one of those doors is empty, that whole **2 in 3 chance moves to the remaining door**, while your own door stays at 1 in 3.

v21.text: Three doors, one prize: you choose a door, then a host who always plays fair opens a different door with nothing behind it. **Switch**, because staying keeps your original odds and switching roughly doubles them.
children: Saying it makes no difference is the classic mistake.

v21.text: Your first guess is a long shot, and the host's reveal tells you nothing new about it. The combined chance held by the other two doors therefore **collapses onto the single door left closed**.
The error comes from seeing two doors and calling it a coin flip, which overlooks that the host **could not** open your door or the prize door.

v22.text: The **Monty Hall 3 Door problem** is a test of how people handle **combinations of events**. You pick a door, the host who always plays fair opens an empty one, and the best move is to **switch**.
children: Always switching wins about **two-thirds** of the time, always staying about **one-third**.

v22.text: Why: the first pick holds a **1 in 3** chance, so the other two doors together hold **2 in 3**. The reveal does not change your door's chance, so all **2 in 3** now sits behind the one remaining door.
Most people say the two doors are equally likely and that it makes no difference. That is **wrong**, because the host's choice of which door to open is not random.

sections.title: Risky Decisions
original: Risky choices depend on how outcomes are framed and perceived. In these choices people pick between a guaranteed outcome and a gamble, where the guaranteed outcome can be a gain or a loss.
In prospect-theory research (Kahneman and Tversky), people typically avoid risk with gains, taking the sure thing, and seek risk with losses, taking the gamble.
So decisions about risk depend on whether outcomes are seen as gains or losses, not only on the objective odds.

v20.text: The main theme is that **risky choices depend on framing**: the way a choice is framed makes a big difference to the decision, even when the situations are **otherwise equivalent**.
children: **Kahneman and Tversky (1982)** summarized many of these **framing effects**.

v20.text: In this research people choose between a **guaranteed outcome** and a **gamble** with a stated chance of winning and a stated chance of losing.
children: The guaranteed outcome can be a gain or a loss, so researchers can see how **risk, stakes, and gain versus loss** affect the choice.

v20.text: In prospect-theory research (Kahneman and Tversky), people typically **avoid risk when the choice is about gains**, taking the sure thing, and **seek risk when the choice is about losses**, taking the gamble.
children: So risky decisions depend on how outcomes are **perceived**, not just on the objective odds.

v21.text: **Risky choices depend on how they are framed**, even when the situations are otherwise equivalent.
The standard setup offers a **sure outcome** against a **gamble**. The sure outcome can be a gain or a loss, which shows how **gain versus loss** changes the choice.

The typical pattern, from prospect-theory research, is **caution with gains** (take the sure thing) and **risk-taking with losses** (take the gamble). Perception of the outcome matters, not just the odds.

v22.text: Kahneman and Tversky (1982) summarized many **framing effects**, in which the same situation described differently draws a different choice, and risky decisions are a prime case.
Researchers set a **guaranteed outcome** against a **gamble** with stated chances of winning and losing, and make the guaranteed outcome either a gain or a loss to see what that does to the choice.

Kahneman and Tversky's prospect-theory work gives the typical result: with gains people **play it safe** and take the sure thing, while with losses they **gamble**. How an outcome is perceived drives the decision, not only the odds.

sections.title: German & Defeyter (2000): Immunity to functional fixedness in young children
original: German and Defeyter (2000) tested whether young children get stuck on an object's usual function (functional fixedness), using a box that was first shown as a container.
Older children (6 and 7) were slower to use the box as a support after seeing it as a container; 5-year-olds were not slowed and were even faster.
Younger children seem to have a more fluid idea of function, so one demonstrated use did not lock the object in.

v20.text: **German and Defeyter (2000)** asked whether young children show **functional fixedness**, being stuck on an object's **usual function** so that a new use is slow or missed.
children: **Duncker's (1945) candle problem** is the classic case: the tack box is hard to see as a platform once it has held the tacks.
Adults show it too (**Adamson, 1952**) and problem solving normally improves with age, so younger children were expected to do worse.
In the box task, a toy bear wanted to reach a toy on a high shelf, and the solution was to turn a box over as a support; in one condition the box had first been used as a container.

v20.text: **Older children (6 and 7) were slower** to use the box as a support once its container use had been shown, while **5-year-olds were immune** and were even faster than the older children in that condition.
children: Without the container demonstration, children simply got better with age.

v20.text: The authors, drawing on **German and Johnson (1997)**, predicted this: **younger children have a more fluid idea of function**, where any goal of the user can make an object's function.
children: Older children hold function more rigidly, so the demonstrated container use has to be **restructured** before the box can become a support.

v21.text: Young children may not get stuck on what an object is usually for, even though adults do and problem solving usually improves with age.
children: German and Defeyter tested this with a toy bear that needed a box turned over as a support to reach a toy on a high shelf, sometimes after the box had been shown as a container.

v21.text: Older children, 6 and 7, were **slowed by the container demonstration**. The **5-year-olds were not**, and solved faster than the older children in that condition.
children: With no demonstration, performance just improved with age.

v21.text: The likely reason is that **young children treat function as flexible**: whatever the user is trying to do can make something a tool.
children: Older children hold a use more firmly and must restructure the problem to see the box as a support.

v22.text: **German and Defeyter (2000)** asked whether children share the **functional fixedness** that **Duncker (1945)** found with the candle problem and **Adamson (1952)** found in adults.
children: Because problem solving improves with age, the general expectation was that younger children would do worse.
Their box task had a toy bear reach a toy on a high shelf by using a box as a support, after the box was or was not shown as a container.

v22.text: **Children of 6 and 7 were slowed** by the container demonstration, but **5-year-olds were immune** and solved faster than the older children in that condition.
children: Without the demonstration, children improved with age.

v22.text: **German and Johnson (1997)** proposed that **young children have a more fluid idea of function**, and German and Defeyter predicted the immunity from it.
children: Older children hold function rigidly and must **restructure** the container use to see a support.

sections.title: Leist et al. (2022): Irrelevant speech impairs serial recall of verbal but not spatial items
original: Leist and colleagues (2022) studied the irrelevant speech effect: speech to be ignored impairs serial recall, more for changing-state speech than steady-state speech.
Speech hurt verbal recall but not spatial recall, in children and adults.
The effect is specific to verbal material, which fits phonological interference better than attention-capture or changing-state accounts.

v20.text: The **irrelevant speech effect** is that speech you are told to ignore **impairs serial recall**, and **changing-state speech** (different syllables) hurts more than **steady-state speech** (one syllable repeated).
children: Accounts differ: speech corrupts **phonological traces** (**Salamé and Baddeley, 1982**), changing sound disrupts **order rehearsal** for any item (**Jones and colleagues**), or sound **captures attention** (**Cowan, 1995**).
**Leist and colleagues (2022)** separated these by testing **verbal** and **spatial** items in children and adults.

v20.text: Speech **impaired verbal recall but not spatial recall**, in both children and adults.
children: Children were more impaired than adults relative to silence, and they were hurt by steady-state speech too, which adults were not.
This did not reproduce **Jones and colleagues' (1995)** report of equal effects on verbal and spatial items.

v20.text: So the effect is **specific to verbal material**.
children: That is hard for **attention-capture** and **changing-state** accounts, which predict spatial disruption too.
It fits **similarity-based interference** between the speech and **phonological representations** of the list.

v21.text: Ignored speech still **disrupts recall of an ordered list**, and speech with changing syllables does more damage than one repeated syllable.
children: Theories disagree about why: it may corrupt sound-based memory traces, break up order rehearsal, or capture attention.

v21.text: The test was whether speech also disrupts memory for **locations**, in children and adults. It **did not**: only **word-like items** suffered.
children: Children were hit harder than adults, even by repeated-syllable speech, although the extra cost of changing syllables was similar in both groups.

v21.text: That points to **interference with sound-based codes** and causes trouble for accounts that predict damage to any kind of item.

v22.text: **Salamé and Baddeley (1982)**, **Jones and colleagues**, and **Cowan (1995)** offered competing explanations of why ignored speech disrupts serial recall: phonological traces, order rehearsal, and attention capture.
children: Changing-state speech does more damage than steady-state speech.

v22.text: **Leist and colleagues (2022)** showed that speech **did not disrupt spatial recall** in either children or adults, only verbal recall, unlike the equal effects reported by **Jones and colleagues (1995)**.
children: Children were more impaired than adults relative to silence, but the added cost of changing-state speech was about the same in both groups.

v22.text: Leist and colleagues concluded the effect is **specific to verbal material**, which challenges the **attention-capture** and **changing-state** accounts and fits **similarity-based interference** with phonological codes.

sections.title: Morrison & Richmond (2020): Offloading items from memory
original: Morrison and Richmond (2020) studied cognitive offloading, using actions like writing things down to reduce mental demands (Risko and Gilbert, 2016).
Offloading improved memory, especially at high loads, and people offloaded more as load grew.
Memory ability did not predict who offloaded, so offloading may be a compensatory strategy across abilities.

v20.text: **Cognitive offloading** is using actions such as writing things down to **reduce the mental demands** of a task (**Risko and Gilbert, 2016**).
children: **Morrison and Richmond (2020)** replicated and extended **Risko and Dunn (2015)**, asking who offloads and whether it helps.
They expected people with **lower working memory capacity** to offload more.

v20.text: **Offloading improved memory**, especially at **high loads** beyond short-term memory capacity, and people **offloaded more as the load grew**, as in Risko and Dunn.
**Memory ability did not predict who offloaded**, which failed to replicate Risko and Dunn, and capacity did not predict the benefit either.
children: So offloading **may be a compensatory strategy** that helps across a wide range of memory ability.

v21.text: Writing things down is a way of **taking load off memory**.
children: The question was whether people use it when they most need it, and whether it works.

v21.text: When lists got longer than memory can hold, people **used the notepad more and remembered more** because of it.
The expected link to **poor memory ability did not appear**: weaker and stronger memories offloaded alike, and gained alike.
children: That suggests offloading **may help people of many abilities**.

v22.text: **Risko and Gilbert (2016)** defined offloading as using actions to reduce a task's mental demands.
children: **Morrison and Richmond (2020)** tested whether people with weaker working memory offload more, as **Risko and Dunn (2015)** had reported.

v22.text: **Morrison and Richmond (2020)** found that offloading helped most at **high loads** and rose with load, matching Risko and Dunn (2015).
They did **not** replicate Risko and Dunn's link between memory ability and offloading, and ability did not predict the benefit, so offloading **may be a compensatory strategy** across abilities.

sections.title: Hoover & Healy (2019): The Bat-and-Ball Problem
original: The bat-and-ball problem (Frederick, 2005): bat and ball cost $1.10 and the bat costs $1.00 more. The intuitive answer is 10 cents; the correct answer is 5 cents.
Kahneman and Frederick (2002) called the error unconscious attribute substitution; De Neys and colleagues (2013) found wrong reasoners were less confident than on a control version.
Hoover and Healy (2019) found wrong reasoners mostly remembered 'more than' and because substitution cannot be confirmed as the cause of the error, they call the sensitivity error sensitivity.

v20.text: In the **bat-and-ball problem** (**Frederick, 2005**), a bat and ball cost $1.10 together and the bat costs $1.00 more than the ball.
children: The intuitive answer is **10 cents**, but then the bat is only 90 cents more.
The correct answer is **5 cents**: ball x, bat x plus $1.00, so x is 5 cents.

v20.text: **Kahneman and Frederick (2002)** explained the error as **unconscious attribute substitution**: reasoners neglect 'more than' and answer an easier question.
children: **De Neys, Rossi and Houdé (2013)** found incorrect reasoners were **less confident** on the standard problem than on a control without 'more than', called **substitution sensitivity**.

v20.text: **Hoover and Healy (2019)**, using matching problems, found that incorrect reasoners mostly **recalled and recognized 'more than'**, so it was not simply overlooked, but they apparently did not use its meaning.
children: Some reasoners did lose the phrase and many stayed very confident, so substitution may still occur for some.
Because they cannot be sure the error was substitution, they prefer the term **error sensitivity**.

v21.text: The **bat-and-ball puzzle** pulls people to answer 10 cents. Subtracting $1.00 from $1.10 leaves the bat only 90 cents more, so the right answer is **5 cents**.
One account says wrong answers come from **swapping in an easier question** without noticing.
children: Evidence for it: wrong reasoners were **less sure of themselves** than on a version without 'more than', as if they sensed a problem.

v21.text: A later study found those reasoners often **still remembered the phrase 'more than'** but apparently did not use it, so the error may be **conscious** rather than hidden.
children: Others lost the phrase or stayed confident, so substitution can still happen for some.
Because the cause cannot be pinned down, the authors call the confidence drop **error sensitivity**.

v22.text: **Frederick (2005)** used the **bat-and-ball problem**: 10 cents feels right, but 5 cents is correct because the bat must cost a dollar more.

**Kahneman and Frederick (2002)** proposed **attribute substitution**, and **De Neys, Rossi and Houdé (2013)** showed wrong reasoners were **less confident** than on a control version, a **substitution sensitivity**.
**Hoover and Healy (2019)** found wrong reasoners mostly **remembered 'more than'** but apparently did not use its meaning, evidence for a **conscious error process**.
children: Because some lost the phrase and many stayed confident, substitution may still occur for some reasoners.
Hoover and Healy prefer **error sensitivity** because they cannot be sure the error was substitution.

sections.title: Giuliani et al. (2023): The joint effect of framing and defaults on choice behavior
original: Giuliani and colleagues (2023) combined the framing effect (sure option for gains, risky option for losses) with the default effect, choosing the preselected option.
A risky default raised risk taking, a sure default did not raise risk aversion, and the two effects were additive.
In an exploratory question asked after the choice, the belief about the default's origin went with following or rejecting it.

v20.text: **Giuliani and colleagues (2023)** combined the **framing effect** (**Tversky and Kahneman, 1981**), where people prefer the **sure option for gains** and the **risky option for losses**, with the **default effect** (**Johnson and Goldstein, 2003**), a tendency to take the **preselected option**.
children: The Asian disease problem is the classic example: 'saved' wording favors the sure program and 'die' wording favors the risky one.
The two effects had mostly been studied separately.

v20.text: People made **life-or-death** and **financial** choices with **no default**, a **sure default**, or a **risky default**.
children: They found a **classic framing effect** and **more risk taking when lives were at stake**, although lives concerned people elsewhere while the money was the participant's own, so involvement differed.
A **risky default raised risk taking**, a **sure default did not raise risk aversion**, and framing and default were **additive**.

v20.text: Afterward people said why they thought the option was preselected. Those who saw it as the **most rational choice** followed it most, **expert advice** left people indifferent, and **previous respondents or chance** went with rejecting it.
children: This question was exploratory and came after the choice, so beliefs may partly justify a choice already made.

v21.text: Two known influences on choice were tested together: **wording** (people take the sure thing when outcomes are gains and gamble when they are losses) and **defaults** (people drift to whatever is preselected).
When choices were about lives or about money, with the sure or the risky option preselected, **wording kept its usual effect** and the effects of wording and default simply **added up**.
children: A **risky default pushed people toward risk**, while a **sure default did not make them more cautious** overall.
Risk was higher when lives were at stake, though involvement also differed from the money case.

v21.text: Why people followed or rejected the default seemed to go with **what they thought it was**: most rational, expert advice, or chance.
children: That was an after-the-fact, exploratory question, so it may reflect justification more than cause.

v22.text: **Giuliani and colleagues (2023)** joined the **framing effect** of **Tversky and Kahneman (1981)** to the **default effect** shown in organ donation by **Johnson and Goldstein (2003)**.
They found a **classic framing effect** and more risk taking with lives than money (as in **Fagley and Miller, 1997**), though lives were another country's and money was the participant's own.
children: A **risky default raised risk taking** while a **sure default did not raise risk aversion** overall, so in some circumstances people are nudged toward risk more easily than toward certainty.
Framing and default effects were **additive**.

v22.text: In **Giuliani and colleagues' (2023)** exploratory question after the choice, belief in the default as **most rational** went with following it most, **expert advice** with indifference, and **previous respondents or chance** with rejection.
children: Beliefs may partly be justification of a choice already made.

sections.title: Chein et al. (2011) and Albert, Chein & Steinberg (2013): Peers and the adolescent brain
original: Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013) argue adolescents reason about risk like adults in the lab, but the peer context is what raises risk taking.
Chein and colleagues (2011) scanned a driving game played alone or watched by friends: adolescents took more risks when watched, with greater reward-region activity.
Cognitive-control regions did not change with peers, so the authors concluded the effect worked mainly through reward circuitry.

v20.text: **Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013)** reviewed why adolescents take more risks in real life although they **reason about risk as well as adults in the lab**.
children: Their answer is the **peer context**, shown by **Gardner and Steinberg (2005)**, where adolescents took more risks with peers present than alone and adults did not.
Peers prime the **reward system** (ventral striatum, orbitofrontal cortex) while the **cognitive-control system** (lateral prefrontal cortex) matures slowly, a **maturational gap**.

v20.text: **Chein and colleagues (2011)** scanned people playing a **driving game** **alone** or **watched by friends** in another room, with no interaction during play.
children: Adolescents took significantly more risks when watched, though the age-by-context difference on behavior was not itself significant in this small sample.
The **ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex** were more active when friends watched, and this went with risky decisions.

v20.text: **Cognitive-control regions** were less engaged in adolescents than adults but did **not change with peers**, so the authors concluded the peer effect works mainly through **reward circuitry**, though the two systems influence each other.
children: People less resistant to peer influence showed a larger reward response; peers also raise preference for **immediate rewards**, even when only believed to be watching.

v21.text: Teens reason about risk about as well as adults when alone, so the extra real-world risk is attributed to **the social setting**.
children: Experiments show teens take more risks with friends present than alone, and adults do not.

v21.text: In a brain-scan driving game, teens played alone or with friends **watching from another room** and not interacting.
children: When watched, **reward areas became more active** in teens and this went with riskier choices, even though the behavior gap between age groups was not itself firm in a small sample.

v21.text: **Control areas did not change with an audience**, so the effect seems to come mainly from **stronger reward response** rather than weaker self-control, although the two systems interact.
children: Peers also push toward immediate rewards, even when only believed to be watching.

v22.text: **Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013)** point to the peer context, citing **Gardner and Steinberg (2005)**, where adolescents, but not adults, took more risks with peers than alone.
children: Their model is a **maturational gap** between a peer-primed **reward system** and a slowly maturing **cognitive-control system**.

v22.text: **Chein, Albert, O'Brien, Uckert and Steinberg (2011)** scanned a **driving game** played alone or watched by friends, and found adolescents took significantly more risks when watched.
children: Reward regions (**ventral striatum, orbitofrontal cortex**) were more active in adolescents when peers watched, going with risky decisions.

v22.text: **Chein and colleagues (2011)** found **cognitive-control regions did not change with peers**, so they concluded the effect works mainly through **reward circuitry**; **Albert and colleagues (2013)** note the two systems interact.
children: **O'Brien et al. (2011)** and **Weigard et al. (2011)** add that peers raise preference for immediate rewards, even when only believed present.
